opus-5.5.text:
I think it's incredibly important, and honestly it's something we've become much more deliberate about over the last couple of years. There's a version of research that can drift into optimizing benchmarks that don't really map to anything people care about. You get a nice number on an eval, you write it up, and then it turns out the capability doesn't hold up when someone actually tries to use it to get work done.

Grounding research in real use cases is a forcing function. When you see how people use these models, whether they're debugging a codebase, doing a long research task, or chaining together a bunch of tool calls, you quickly find where the models break. Maybe it's long-horizon coherence, maybe it's knowing when to ask for clarification versus pushing ahead, maybe it's recovering gracefully from a failed step. Those failure modes are often much more interesting and much more important than whatever the leaderboard says.

At the same time, I don't think you want research to be purely reactive to product. Some of the biggest leaps came from people pursuing a primitive because they believed in it, like scaling, reinforcement learning on reasoning, and so on, before there was an obvious product for it. So the way I think about it is as a loop. Fundamental research creates new capabilities, product and agentic deployments stress-test those capabilities in the real world, and that feedback tells you which research directions really matter next.

Agents especially make this loop tighter. With a chat model you can get away with being impressive in a single turn. With an agent, the model has to be reliable across dozens or hundreds of steps, and small error rates compound. That pushes you toward research on reliability, calibration, and planning, which I think are some of the most important problems in the field right now. So yes, I'd say connecting the two isn't just nice to have. It's one of the main ways we figure out what to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says connecting research to practical use cases is incredibly important, but does not say that this connection is underappreciated.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's incredibly important, and honestly, I'd say it's become one of the central organizing principles for how we think about research now.

For a long time there was this clean separation: research people push the frontier on benchmarks, and then some other team figures out what to do with it. And that worked okay when the models were mostly chat. But once you move into agentic use cases, where a model is operating a browser, writing and running code, or carrying out a multi-step task over hours, the gap between "it scores well" and "it actually works for someone" gets enormous. You discover failure modes you would never have found on a static eval. The model loses track of state, it doesn't know when to ask for clarification, it's overconfident about something it half-did.

So the product surface becomes a research instrument. It's the thing that tells you what the real frontier is, as opposed to the one you imagine from the leaderboard. Codex is a good example for us. A lot of what we learned about long-horizon reliability, about how to structure tool use, about how the model should communicate what it did, came directly from watching real engineers hand it real tasks and seeing where it fell over. That feedback loop then shapes what we train on and what we measure.

The other piece is that it keeps you honest about what matters. It's easy in research to get seduced by a capability that's impressive but not load-bearing for anyone. When you're grounded in actual use cases, you end up prioritizing things like reliability, calibration, and recovery from mistakes, which are less flashy but are actually what unlocks the next tier of usefulness.

So I'd frame it less as "research should serve product" and more as the two being parts of the same loop. The primitives tell you what's possible, the products tell you what's true, and you need both to move fast in the right direction.

r001.rationale: The response calls the connection incredibly important and central to research, but does not say it is underappreciated or underestimated.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s really important. When you’re doing research, you have these primitives—reasoning, tool use, memory—and you can measure progress on each one independently. But putting them together into a product forces you to ask whether they actually help someone accomplish something useful.

That’s especially true with agents. A model can do well on an individual task, but if it needs to take twenty steps, recover from mistakes, and know when to ask the user for clarification, you start to see a different set of challenges. Those are research problems, too, and you don’t always discover them until you try the real workflow.

So I see it as a feedback loop. Research opens up new product possibilities, and building those products tells you where the research needs to go next. You still want room for exploratory work, but that connection to actual use is incredibly valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says connecting research to real products is important and valuable, but does not say that this connection is underappreciated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s really important. When you’re working on a research primitive, you usually have some benchmark that tells you whether it’s improving. But putting it into a product exposes a different set of questions: Is it reliable enough? Does it know when to ask for clarification? Can it recover when something goes wrong?

Agentic use cases make that connection especially valuable, because success depends on a whole sequence of decisions. You can have a model that’s very good at each individual step and still have an experience that breaks down over a longer task. So you want a tight feedback loop between research and actual use. Research opens up new possibilities, and trying to make those possibilities useful tells you what research problems to tackle next.

r001.rationale: The response says connecting research primitives to products is “really important,” but does not say this connection is underappreciated.
